deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E260 Euler assumes that the friction a moving fluid exerts on a tube wall is proportional to the local pressure, as in Coulomb's law for solid friction, with coefficient α. The pressure here is total pressure, including the atmospheric head l ≈ 30 ft of water. Integrating along a horizontal tube BC of length b and 'amplitude' (cross-section) gg gives an exponential factor 𝔅 = e^{-αb/g}. In the steady-flow limit, the head due to the efflux velocity through the small orifice CC is v = a𝔅 − (1−𝔅)l, i.e. v = a − (a+l)(1−e^{-αb/g}). Because the friction also acts on the atmospheric part of the pressure, there is a threshold: water flows only if a e^{-αb/g} > l(1−e^{-αb/g}).

§82: Euler prefers this threshold method for measuring α over the earlier capillary-tube method. Capillary tubes have 'singular properties' (capillarity), which might contaminate the value of α.

§83, worked example: a very wide vessel (so αa/f is negligible), b = 2 ft, g = 1/25 ft, and a negligible orifice (𝔤 = k⁴/g⁴ ≈ 0). With α = 1/4000, αb/g = 1/80, so 𝔅 ≈ 1 − 1/80. Then v = a − (a+30)/80 = (79a−30)/80, and outflow requires a > 30/79 ft.

§84: α = 1/6000 gives 𝔅 = 1 − 1/120, v = (119a−30)/120 and threshold a > 30/119 ft. In general 𝔅 = 1 − 50α and v = a(1−50α) − 1500α. One slowly raises the head until flow just starts and records a; then α = a/(50a+1500).

§85 (continued on the next page): for any tube with αb/g small, α = ag/(b(a+l)). This is the linearization of the exact threshold condition αb/g = log(1 + a/l) − (small terms) from the previous page.
errors: In §83 and §84 the printed intermediate expressions a − (a−30)/80 and a − (a−30)/120 should read a − (a+30)/80 and a − (a+30)/120. The final forms (79a−30)/80 and (119a−30)/120 are correct, as is the general formula v = a(1−αb/g) − αbl/g on the next page. This is a sign misprint.
𝔅 = e^{-1/80} is replaced by 1 − 1/80. This is a first-order approximation, harmless here.

Physically, the friction hypothesis (wall shear proportional to absolute pressure, atmosphere included) is wrong for liquids. The predicted no-flow threshold for a horizontal tube does not exist for real water; real resistance is viscous or turbulent and depends on velocity. The measuring method proposed is therefore unsound, though internally consistent. Euler himself notes in §79 that gravity in the tube is ignored.

ideas.what: Wall friction proportional to local pressure, producing exponential decay of pressure along a pipe, 𝔅 = e^{-αb/g}
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb-type (pressure-dependent) wall friction; the same exponential structure as Janssen's silo law for granular media
ideas.usually_credited_to: Coulomb (solid friction, 1781); Janssen (1895) for the exponential pressure law in granular columns
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Commentarii 6 (1761); discussed by Truesdell in his Opera omnia II.12–13 introduction (Rational fluid mechanics 1687–1765)

ideas.what: A no-flow threshold head, and its use to measure the friction coefficient: α = a/(50a+1500), generally α = ag/(b(a+l))
ideas.modern_name: Yield/threshold condition, analogous to static friction or yield stress
ideas.usually_credited_to: Not a recognized method (physically invalid for water)

ideas.what: Rejecting capillary tubes for measuring friction because of their peculiar properties
ideas.modern_name: Awareness of capillary or surface effects as a systematic error

missed.claim: Euler's 'frictional fluid' in a pipe is mathematically a Coulomb-frictional (granular-like) material. Wall shear proportional to normal pressure yields exponential attenuation of pressure along the conduit and a finite threshold driving head. This is the same structure as Janssen's 1895 silo law and as plug flow with Coulomb wall friction in modern granular and powder transport. Euler's analysis is a mid-18th-century instance of that model, though he misapplied it to water.
missed.quote: 𝔅 = e^{-αb/g} ... Vt igitur aqua hoc casu actu effluat, necesse est, vt sit a > 30/79 pedis
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is a historical precursor for pressure-dependent wall friction in granular or plug flows. The usual narrative treats E260 only as a failed theory of fluid resistance and does not link it to granular mechanics. This is of modest historical interest only.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a numerical illustration of a known, physically mistaken friction hypothesis that Truesdell has already discussed. The only novelty is the loose Janssen/granular analogy, along with a small sign misprint.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces the printed 'a − (a−30)/80' and 'a − (a−30)/120'. These match the original but are misprints for (a+30) in the original itself.
Page header: the image shows '369'; the transcription is consistent.
